diameter-of-binary-tree.pattern: Tree DP: return height upwards, update the best "left height + right height" at each node

approaches.name: Compute both heights separately at every node
approaches.idea: The longest path through a node uses the height of its left subtree plus the height of its right subtree. Compute those heights from scratch at each node and take the best.
steps: `height(t)`: 0 for null, else `1 + max(height(left), height(right))`.
For every node, candidate = `height(left) + height(right)`.
Return the largest candidate over all nodes.
approaches.why: Heights are recomputed for every ancestor: O(n·h), O(n²) for a chain.

approaches.name: One DFS returning heights
approaches.idea: A single post-order DFS returns each subtree's height to its parent; at each node, `leftHeight + rightHeight` is the longest path bending there, so update a running best.
steps: `height(t)`: 0 for null.
Compute `l = height(left)`, `r = height(right)`; update `best = max(best, l + r)`.
Return `1 + max(l, r)`. The answer is `best`.
approaches.why: Each node is visited once; the recursion is as deep as the tree.

house-robber-iii.pattern: Tree DP returning two values per node: best if robbed, best if skipped

approaches.name: Rob this house or not, recursively
approaches.idea: Either rob the root (then skip its children and continue from its grandchildren) or skip it (and solve both children freely). Take the better.
steps: `best(t)`: 0 for null.
Rob: `t.val + best(grandchildren…)` (the four grandchildren).
Skip: `best(t.left) + best(t.right)`. Return the larger.
approaches.why: Each node is solved again from its parent and from its grandparent, so work grows exponentially with depth.

approaches.name: Same recursion with a memo per node
approaches.idea: Cache `best(t)` in a hash map keyed by the node, so every subtree is solved once.
steps: Same recurrence as the brute force.
Store each node's result in a map and return it on repeat visits.
approaches.why: n distinct subproblems; the map holds n entries.

approaches.name: Return (robbed, skipped) for each subtree
approaches.idea: Let each call return two numbers: the best for its subtree if its root is robbed, and if it is not. The parent combines them directly — no map needed.
steps: With `(lr, ls) = dfs(left)` and `(rr, rs) = dfs(right)`: robbed = `val + ls + rs`; skipped = `max(lr, ls) + max(rr, rs)`.
Return `max(robbed, skipped)` for the root.
approaches.why: One post-order pass; only the recursion stack is used.

longest-zigzag-path-in-a-binary-tree.pattern: Tree DP carrying the zigzag length that arrived from each direction

approaches.name: Walk a zigzag from every node in both directions
approaches.idea: From each node, follow the zigzag starting left and starting right, alternating until a child is missing, and record the longest.
steps: For each node, walk: go left, then right, then left… counting edges; then do the same starting with right.
Keep the longest walk over all nodes and both directions.
approaches.why: Each of the n nodes walks down at most h levels in each direction.

approaches.name: DFS carrying the length of the zigzag that arrives here
approaches.idea: Pass down two numbers: the zigzag length if we arrived by going left, and if we arrived by going right. Going left from here continues a path that arrived going right (+1), and starts fresh for the other direction.
steps: `dfs(t, cameLeft, cameRight)`: update the best with both values.
Go to the left child with `(cameRight + 1, 0)`: continuing the zigzag that came from the right, or starting over.
Go to the right child with `(0, cameLeft + 1)`.
Start with `dfs(root, 0, 0)`.
approaches.why: Each node is visited once; the recursion is h deep.

predict-the-winner.pattern: Interval minimax DP on the score difference

approaches.name: Recursion on the best score difference
approaches.idea: Let `diff(i, j)` be the best (my score − opponent's score) the player to move can get from `nums[i..j]`. Taking an end gives that number minus whatever the opponent then achieves on the rest.
steps: `diff(i, j)`: if `i == j`, return `nums[i]`.
Return `max(nums[i] − diff(i + 1, j), nums[j] − diff(i, j − 1))`.
Player 1 wins (or ties) when `diff(0, n − 1) >= 0`.
approaches.why: Two choices per move over n moves, with repeated ranges.

approaches.name: Memoisation on the range
approaches.idea: There are only n(n + 1)/2 ranges, so cache `diff(i, j)`.
steps: Same recurrence as the brute force.
Cache each range's result in an n × n table.
approaches.why: Each range is computed once with O(1) work.

approaches.name: Bottom-up with one row
approaches.idea: Fill ranges by increasing start from the end: `dp[j]` holds `diff(i + 1, j)` before it is updated to `diff(i, j)`, and `dp[j − 1]` is already `diff(i, j − 1)`.
steps: For `i` from n − 1 down to 0: `dp[i] = nums[i]`; for `j` from `i + 1`: `dp[j] = max(nums[i] − dp[j], nums[j] − dp[j − 1])`.
Return `dp[n − 1] >= 0`.
approaches.why: Same n²/2 ranges in one row of memory.

minimum-score-triangulation-of-polygon.pattern: Interval DP: the edge (i, j) belongs to one triangle (i, k, j); split there

approaches.name: Recursion over the third vertex of edge (i, j)
approaches.idea: In any triangulation of the polygon `i..j`, the side `(i, j)` is in exactly one triangle `(i, k, j)`. That triangle splits the rest into two smaller polygons `i..k` and `k..j`. Try every `k`.
steps: `best(i, j)`: 0 if `j − i < 2` (no triangle possible).
Return the minimum over `k` in `(i, j)` of `best(i, k) + values[i]·values[k]·values[j] + best(k, j)`.
Answer `best(0, n − 1)`.
approaches.why: Without caching it explores every triangulation — the Catalan number Cₙ₋₂ of them, which grows like 4ⁿ.

approaches.name: Bottom-up interval DP
approaches.idea: Compute `dp[i][j]` for every sub-polygon, from short gaps to long ones, using the same split rule.
steps: `dp[i][j] = 0` when `j − i < 2`.
For `gap` from 2 to n − 1, for each `i` with `j = i + gap`: `dp[i][j] = min over k of dp[i][k] + v[i]·v[k]·v[j] + dp[k][j]`.
Return `dp[0][n − 1]`.
approaches.why: n²/2 intervals, each trying up to n split points. Scores stay below 49 × 100³ ≈ 5·10⁷, so 32-bit ints suffice.

binary-tree-maximum-path-sum.pattern: Tree DP: return the best downward branch, combine both branches at each node

approaches.name: At every node, recompute its best downward branches
approaches.idea: The best path whose highest node is `t` is `t.val` plus the best non-negative downward path from each child. Compute those downward paths from scratch at every node.
steps: `down(t)`: the best sum of a path starting at `t` going down = `t.val + max(0, down(left), down(right))`.
For every node: candidate = `t.val + max(0, down(left)) + max(0, down(right))`.
Return the largest candidate.
approaches.why: `down` is recomputed for every ancestor of a node: O(n·h).

approaches.name: One post-order DFS
approaches.idea: Compute each node's best downward branch once, bottom-up. At the node, the best path that peaks there uses both branches (each only if positive); the parent can only continue one branch.
steps: `gain(t)`: 0 for null. `l = max(0, gain(left))`, `r = max(0, gain(right))`.
Update `best = max(best, t.val + l + r)`.
Return `t.val + max(l, r)` to the parent.
Start `best` at −∞ so all-negative trees work.
approaches.why: Each node once; the recursion is h deep.

binary-tree-cameras.pattern: Tree DP / greedy from the leaves up with three states (covered, has camera, needs cover)

approaches.name: Try every set of camera nodes
approaches.idea: List the nodes, try every subset as the set of cameras (smallest first), and return the first size that covers every node.
steps: Collect the nodes with their parent and children indices.
For each subset (bitmask) of nodes, check that every node has a camera on itself, its parent or a child.
Return the smallest number of cameras among covering subsets.
approaches.why: Every subset of the n nodes is checked in O(n). Only usable for tiny trees.

approaches.name: Greedy from the leaves up
approaches.idea: A leaf should never hold a camera: putting it on the leaf's parent covers strictly more. So work bottom-up with three states per node — 0: not covered yet, 1: has a camera, 2: covered without a camera. Place a camera at a node exactly when some child is not covered.
steps: `state(null) = 2` (a missing child needs nothing).
If either child is 0 (uncovered), put a camera here: count it and return 1.
If either child has a camera, return 2 (covered). Otherwise return 0 (let the parent cover it).
After the DFS, if the root returned 0, add one camera for it.
approaches.why: One post-order pass. The greedy choice is safe: covering an uncovered child with a camera at its parent covers the parent and grandparent too, which no other placement beats.

burst-balloons.pattern: Interval DP on the LAST balloon burst in each range

approaches.name: Try every bursting order
approaches.idea: Recursively choose which balloon to burst next from those remaining, adding its coins (with its current neighbours), and keep the best total.
steps: Keep the remaining balloons in a list.
For each position `i`: coins = `left · nums[i] · right` (1 past the ends); remove it, recurse, put it back.
Return the best total.
approaches.why: n! orders, each step rebuilding the list. Only feasible for a handful of balloons.

approaches.name: Interval DP choosing the last balloon
approaches.idea: Pad the array with 1 on both ends. For an open range `(l, r)`, choose which balloon `k` bursts LAST inside it: at that moment its neighbours are exactly `l` and `r`, and the two sides `(l, k)` and `(k, r)` were solved independently before.
steps: Let `a = [1] + nums + [1]`; `dp[l][r]` = best coins from bursting everything strictly between `l` and `r`.
For gaps from 2 up to n + 1, for each `l` with `r = l + gap`: `dp[l][r] = max over k in (l, r) of dp[l][k] + a[l]·a[k]·a[r] + dp[k][r]`.
Return `dp[0][n + 1]`.
approaches.why: n²/2 ranges, each trying up to n last balloons. Thinking about the first burst instead makes the sides depend on each other; the last burst is what makes them independent.

minimum-cost-to-cut-a-stick.pattern: Interval DP over sorted cut positions (the first cut in a piece splits it into two subproblems)

approaches.name: Recursion over which cut to make first in each piece
approaches.idea: For a piece between two positions, choose which of its cuts to make first: it costs the piece's length and splits it into two independent pieces. Try every choice.
steps: Sort the cuts and add the ends 0 and n.
`cost(i, j)`: 0 if there is no cut strictly between `points[i]` and `points[j]`.
Otherwise `points[j] − points[i] + min over k in (i, j) of cost(i, k) + cost(k, j)`.
approaches.why: Without caching it explores every order of cutting, which grows like the Catalan numbers in m (the number of cuts).

approaches.name: Bottom-up interval DP
approaches.idea: With the sorted points `0, cuts…, n`, compute `dp[i][j]` (cheapest way to make every cut strictly between points `i` and `j`) for short ranges first.
steps: Build `p = [0] + sorted(cuts) + [n]`; let `k = p.length`.
For gaps from 2 to k − 1, for each `i` with `j = i + gap`: `dp[i][j] = p[j] − p[i] + min over mid in (i, j) of dp[i][mid] + dp[mid][j]`.
Return `dp[0][k − 1]`.
approaches.why: m = number of cuts (≤ 100): m²/2 ranges × m split points. The stick length n (up to 10⁶) never enters the complexity.

stone-game.pattern: Interval DP on score difference (and a parity argument)

approaches.name: Recursive minimax on the row
approaches.idea: Let `diff(i, j)` be the best (current player − opponent) difference on piles `i..j`. Taking the left pile gains `piles[i]` and hands `i + 1..j` to the opponent; same for the right.
steps: `diff(i, i) = piles[i]`.
`diff(i, j) = max(piles[i] − diff(i + 1, j), piles[j] − diff(i, j − 1))`.
Return `diff(0, n − 1) > 0`.
approaches.why: Two choices per move and no caching: the same sub-row is solved many times. Fine for 8 piles, hopeless for 500.

approaches.name: Interval DP table
approaches.idea: The same recurrence, filled for all intervals by increasing length so every sub-row is solved once.
steps: `dp[i][i] = piles[i]`.
For each length from 2 to `n`, and each start `i` with `j = i + len − 1`: `dp[i][j] = max(piles[i] − dp[i + 1][j], piles[j] − dp[i][j − 1])`.
Return `dp[0][n − 1] > 0`.
approaches.why: n² / 2 intervals, O(1) each. This is the general technique: it also works when ties are possible or the pile count is odd, where the parity trick below does not apply.

approaches.name: Alice always wins
approaches.idea: Number the piles 0..n − 1. With an even count, Alice can take every even-index pile or every odd-index pile, whichever set is bigger, and the totals differ because the sum is odd.
steps: Note that Alice, moving first on an even row, can always take the end that keeps her on her chosen parity, and Bob is then forced onto the other parity.
One of the two parity sets holds more stones (the total is odd, so they cannot be equal).
Return `true`.
approaches.why: The argument shows a winning strategy exists, which is all the question asks. In an interview, show the DP first and then point out this observation; it depends entirely on "even count, odd total".

stone-game-ii.pattern: Game DP over (position, M) with suffix sums

approaches.name: Recursive minimax without caching
approaches.idea: From position `i` with parameter `M`, try every `X` in `1..2M`; your total is what remains minus the opponent's best from `i + X` with `max(M, X)`.
steps: Precompute `suffix[i]`, the stones in piles `i..n − 1`.
`best(i, M)`: if `i + 2M >= n`, take everything (`suffix[i]`).
Otherwise return the maximum over `X` of `suffix[i] − best(i + X, max(M, X))`.
approaches.why: States repeat across many move orders and nothing is cached. It works for a handful of piles only.

approaches.name: Memoised (i, M) table
approaches.idea: There are only n × n distinct states (M never needs to exceed n), so cache `best(i, M)` and the whole game is solved once per state.
steps: Precompute suffix sums.
Fill `dp[i][m]` for `i` from `n − 1` down to 0 and `m` from 1 to `n`: if `i + 2m >= n`, `dp[i][m] = suffix[i]`; otherwise the best over `X` of `suffix[i] − dp[i + X][min(n, max(m, X))]`.
Return `dp[0][1]`.
approaches.why: n² states, each trying up to 2M ≤ 2n moves. With n ≤ 100 that is about 10⁶ steps. "Maximise mine" equals "minimise theirs" because all stones in the suffix are split between the two players.
